h: Little drivers, hidden stations and the Covent Garden buzz
p: Got under-sevens in tow? Look out for the dedicated play area for younger children, where they can drive, steer and clamber to their heart's content. Older kids tend to love the simulators and the chance to sit in a driver's seat, while grown-ups can lose an hour in the poster collection alone. London Transport's posters and the famous roundel shaped how the city looks, and you'll recognise more of them than you'd expect.

Allow around two hours for a comfortable visit, a little longer with young train fans who won't be rushed past a single carriage. The shop is a treat too, packed with Tube map gifts, books and models.

Want to go further? The museum also runs Hidden London, a programme of tours exploring disused Underground stations and forgotten corners of the network. They're hugely popular and sell out quickly, so keep an eye out if that sounds like your kind of thing. The museum's depot in Acton, which stores much of the wider collection, opens to visitors on special days throughout the year.

Being on the piazza puts you right in the middle of Covent Garden's buzz. Watch the street performers outside St Paul's Church, browse the stalls and shops in the old market building, or head up to Seven Dials for independent shops and places to eat. The Royal Opera House is next door, and theatreland surrounds you, so it's easy to finish the day with a show. Covent Garden and Leicester Square tube stations are both a short walk away.
